# Tidal Locking and Its Profound Influence on Planetary Climates

Tidal locking occurs when a planet's rotation period matches its orbital period, causing one hemisphere to face its star permanently. This phenomenon, common among planets orbiting red dwarf stars, creates some of the most extreme and fascinating climates in the universe.

The most obvious consequence is the dramatic temperature contrast between hemispheres. The dayside, bathed in perpetual starlight, can reach temperatures hot enough to melt lead, while the nightside plunges to hundreds of degrees below zero, potentially freezing atmospheres onto the surface. Yet this stark division doesn't necessarily doom a planet to uninhabitability.

Atmospheric and oceanic circulation can redistribute heat remarkably effectively. On planets with substantial atmospheres, winds transport energy from the dayside to the nightside, moderating temperature extremes. Climate models of tidally locked worlds suggest that a dense enough atmosphere—perhaps a few bars of pressure—could maintain habitable temperatures across the entire surface. Oceans serve as even better heat reservoirs, potentially creating a temperate ring at the terminator, the twilight zone between day and night.

These circulation patterns also produce exotic weather. The dayside heats air that rises and flows toward the nightside, creating permanent storms and supersonic winds on some worlds. Precipitation may fall perpetually on the dayside, while the nightside accumulates vast ice sheets that, if too massive, could trap atmospheric gases and collapse the atmosphere entirely
